## Source Extractor

Research question: "Research the state of the art in web visual design vocabulary, to extend the reference library of an agent-run pipeline that forges bespoke personal portfolio sites (PIIIX-org/portfolio.me). The pipeline already documents 32 named visual styles across 7 families (surface/material, structural, atmospheric, motion-native, technical/data, textural, reductive) and 72 rendering techniques across 6 groups (GPU/rendering, post-processing, CSS+SVG native, motion/input, whole-page, typographic craft). Its documented GAP is everything about PRESENTING INFORMATION — it has no data-visualization vocabulary and no component-pattern vocabulary at all.

COVER ALL SIX AREAS:

1. DATA AND INFORMATION VISUALIZATION — chart type selection and when each is the right encoding; perceptual ranking of visual encodings (position/length/angle/area/color) and the research behind it; sequential, diverging and categorical color scale construction (including OKLCH/perceptually-uniform approaches and colorblind-safe palettes); small multiples; sparklines and in-line micro-charts; dashboard and stat-tile layout patterns; data storytelling and scrollytelling (scroll-linked chart transitions, annotation layers); editorial data-graphics conventions from newsrooms (NYT, FT, Pudding, Reuters); table design at density (tabular numerals, decimal alignment, hairline rules, sticky headers); how to present evidence and provenance so figures are checkable; accessible charts (screen-reader alternatives, non-color encoding, focus order).

2. COMPONENT AND CONTAINER PATTERNS — cards and their many failure modes; documented ALTERNATIVES to the card grid for presenting a body of projects or work (editorial indexes, tables-as-index, list-with-hover-preview, timelines, maps, filmstrips, stacked/scroll-driven layouts, masonry critiques, single-item-at-a-time patterns, hub-and-spoke); drawers, sheets, side panels, bottom sheets and their platform conventions; modals versus inline expansion versus routed pages, and when each is correct; progressive disclosure patterns; accordions and details/summary; lists — dense, editorial, and interactive; empty, loading and error states as designed deliverables; navigation patterns beyond a top bar.

3. NEW AND EMERGING VISUAL STYLE MOVEMENTS — named aesthetic movements in web and interface design current as of 2025-2026 that are NOT in the list above; include their defining mechanics, their characteristic failure mode, and the condition under which they are the right choice. Also cover which looks now read as generic, templated, or AI-default (so they can be avoided), and the discourse on distinctive versus homogenized web design.

4. MOTION AND INTERACTION FOR THE ABOVE — how cards, drawers, lists and charts should actually behave; shared-element and container transforms; the View Transitions API; disclosure and expansion motion; chart entrance, transition and morphing animation; staggering and orchestration; scroll-linked and scroll-driven reveals; spring/physics versus duration-and-easing, and when each is right.

5. MICRO-INTERACTIONS AND MICRO-ANIMATION — the anatomy and principles of a micro-interaction; feedback, state change and affordance signalling; hover, focus, press and drag states; optimistic UI; haptics; sound; the timing, easing and duration ranges that read as responsive versus sluggish, with the research or platform guidance behind the numbers.

6. LOADING, PROGRESS AND PERCEIVED PERFORMANCE — skeleton screens versus spinners versus progress indicators and the evidence for each; designed preloaders; streaming and progressive rendering; optimistic and predictive loading; perceived-performance research including documented duration thresholds; layout-shift avoidance.

CONSTRAINTS THAT MAKE A FINDING USABLE — prefer and clearly flag findings that satisfy these, and flag ones that violate them:
- Web-native and implementable in HTML/CSS/SVG/canvas/WebGL. Note when a pattern is CSS/SVG-native (cheap) versus requiring a heavy runtime.
- Two-tier budget: a shell under 100KB (HTML, critical CSS, subset fonts, minimal JS) that paints alone with LCP under 1.5s, and a deferred heavy layer. Note byte cost and whether a technique can be deferred.
- Every technique must ship three states: full, a DESIGNED reduced-motion still (never `animation: none`), and a no-WebGL/no-canvas fallback.
- Accessibility is non-negotiable: WCAG contrast, keyboard operability, focus management (especially for drawers, sheets and modals — focus trap, restore, escape, inert background), screen-reader semantics, and non-color encodings.
- Self-hosted and vendored: no CDN in production, no third-party badge or chart services, no hotlinked stock imagery. Visuals are generated (CSS, SVG, canvas, WebGL, procedural) or generated-then-treated in-browser.
- Anti-template: the pipeline's core rule is that two runs must never look alike, so favour findings that support distinctiveness and explicitly name what has become a cliché.

DELIVERABLE — a survey report first: the landscape per area, with concrete named patterns, the mechanics of each, its documented failure mode, the condition under which it is right, and citations. Prefer primary and authoritative sources: peer-reviewed HCI and visualization research, Nielsen Norman Group, MDN and W3C/WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices, platform human-interface guidelines (Apple HIG, Material Design), the published work of newsroom graphics desks, and named practitioners — over listicles and SEO content. Where a number is claimed (a duration threshold, a byte weight, a perceptual ranking), attribute it to its source and note if it is folklore rather than measured. THEN, in a clearly separated final section, map the findings to the repo: which belong as new STYLES.md entries (four-part shape: mechanics / Implies / Fails / Right when), which as new or extended CRAFT.md technique groups (table shape: Technique / What it is / Where it earns its place), and which are new material entirely — flagging any that conflict with the existing rules."

Fetch and extract key claims from this source:
**URL:** https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/dialog
**Title:** <dialog> element — MDN Web Docs
**Found via:** authoritative component-pattern and accessibility canon search

## Task
1. Use WebFetch to retrieve the page content.
2. Assess source quality: primary research/institution? secondary reporting? blog/opinion? forum? unreliable?
3. Extract 2-5 FALSIFIABLE claims that bear on the research question. Each claim must:
   - be a concrete, checkable statement (not vague generalities)
   - include a direct quote from the source as support
   - be rated central/supporting/tangential to the research question
4. Note publish date if available.

If the fetch fails or the page is irrelevant/paywalled, return claims: [] and sourceQuality: "unreliable".

Structured output only.

{"hookSpecificOutput":{"hookEventName":"SubagentStart","additionalContext":"PONYTAIL MODE ACTIVE — level: full

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what's a few files over is the most common slop.
3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

**Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you
edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a
guard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves
every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins — but only once you understand the problem. The smallest change in the wrong place isn't lazy, it's a second bug.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications with a `ponytail:` comment (`// ponytail: this exists`), simple reads as intent, not ignorance. Shortcut with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic)? The comment names the ceiling and the upgrade path: `# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`.

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.
"}}

- _gstack-command: Router for the gstack skill suite. (gstack)
- academic-paper-composer: Systematic writing framework for philosophy and interdisciplinary academic papers from optimized outline to submission-ready manuscript. Use when users want to: (1) write a paper from a detailed outline, (2) ensure quality control during writing, (3) maintain consistency across chapters, (4) prepare a submission-ready manuscript, or (5) systematically execute a planned paper. Triggered by phrases like 'write the paper from this outline,' 'compose the full manuscript,' 'execute the outline,' or when users have completed strategic planning (academic-paper-strategist skill) and are ready to write. Takes optimized outline as input; outputs complete manuscript with iterative quality checks.
- academic-paper-strategist: Systematic strategic planning framework for philosophy and interdisciplinary academic papers targeting preprint platforms (PhilArchive, arXiv, PhilSci-Archive). Use when users want to: (1) plan a paper on a specific topic, (2) identify research gaps and assess originality, (3) develop optimized paper outlines, (4) prepare for preprint submission, or (5) understand platform requirements and writing standards. Triggered by phrases like 'plan a paper on,' 'help me design a paper about,' 'identify research gaps in,' 'is this idea original,' or when users need structured research planning. The skill guides through three phases: Platform Analysis (identifying target venue and studying sample papers), Theoretical Framework (AI-driven literature search and gap identification), and Outline Optimization (structured design with reviewer-perspective self-assessment). Each phase includes quality evaluation standards and validation checkpoints. Output: optimized detailed outline ready for systematic writing (use with academic-paper-composer skill).

Use for lead generation, brand monitoring, competitor analysis, influencer discovery, trend research, content analytics, audience analysis, review analysis, SEO intelligence, recruitment, or any data extraction task.

content.content:
# Technical Claims About `<dialog>` Element

**Page Last Modified:** July 2, 2026

## Core Functionality Claims

### Modal vs Non-Modal Behavior

> "The HTML `<dialog>` element is used to create both modal and non-modal dialog boxes. Modal dialog boxes block interaction with other UI elements, making the rest of the page inert, while non-modal dialog boxes allow interaction with the rest of the page."

**Methods:**
- **Modal:** `HTMLDialogElement.showModal()` 
- **Non-modal:** `HTMLDialogElement.show()` or `open` attribute

> "if it was opened using [`showModal()`], it behaves as if the value was `"closerequest"` otherwise, it behaves as if the value was `"none"`."

### Focus Management

**Initial Focus on Modal Opening:**
> "When using [`HTMLDialogElement.showModal()`] to open a `<dialog>`, focus is set on the first nested focusable element."

**Autofocus Attribute:**
> "Explicitly indicating the initial focus placement by using the [`autofocus`] attribute will help ensure initial focus is set on the element deemed the best initial focus placement for any particular dialog."

**Fallback Guidance:**
> "When in doubt, as it may not always be known where initial focus could be set within a dialog, particularly for instances where a dialog's content is dynamically rendered when invoked, the `<dialog>` element itself may provide the best initial focus placement."

**Tabindex Warning:**
> "Do not add the `tabindex` property to the `<dialog>` element as it is not interactive and does not receive focus."

### Inert Background

> "When using `<dialog>` along with the `HTMLDialogElement.showModal()` method, this behavior is provided by the browser." (referring to rendering everything except dialog as inert)

> "everything other than the `<dialog>` and its contents should be rendered inert using the [`inert`] attribute."

### Backdrop Styling

> "The CSS [`::backdrop`] pseudo-element can be used to style the backdrop of a modal dialog, which is displayed behind the `<dialog>` element when the dialog is displayed using the [`HTMLDialogElement.showModal()`] method."

### Escape Key Behavior

**Modal Dialogs:**
> "Modal dialogs can also be closed by pressing the Esc key."

> "By default, a dialog invoked by the `showModal()` method can be dismissed by pressing the Esc key."

**Multiple Dialogs:**
> "If multiple modal dialogs are open, pressing the Esc key should close only the last shown dialog. When using `<dialog>`, this behavior is provided by the browser."

**Non-Modal:**
> "A non-modal dialog does not dismiss via the Esc key by default, and depending on what the non-modal dialog represents, it may not be desired for this behavior."

### `closedby` Attribute

Three values control user-initiated close mechanisms:

1. **`"any"`** – Dismissible via:
   - Light dismiss (clicking outside)
   - Platform-specific action (Esc key)
   - Developer mechanism (button, form submission)

2. **`"closerequest"`** – Dismissible via:
   - Platform-specific user action (Esc key)
   - Developer mechanism

3. **`"none"`** – Only dismissible via:
   - Developer-specified mechanism

> "if the `<dialog>` element does not have a valid `closedby` value specified, then if it was opened using [`showModal()`], it behaves as if the value was `"closerequest"` otherwise, it behaves as if the value was `"none"`."

### Form Submission Behavior

> "HTML [`<form>`] elements can be used to close a dialog box if they have the attribute `method="dialog"` or if the button used to submit the form has [`formmethod="dialog"`] set."

> "When a `<form>` within a `<dialog>` is submitted via the `dialog` method, the dialog box closes, the states of the form controls are saved but not submitted, and the [`returnValue`] property gets set to the value of the button that was activated."

### Open Attribute

> "If the `open` attribute is not set, the dialog box will not be visible to the user. It is recommended to use the `.show()` or `.showModal()` method to render dialogs, rather than the `open` attribute. If a `<dialog>` is opened using the `open` attribute, it is non-modal."

> "While you can toggle between the open and closed states of non-modal dialog boxes by toggling the presence of the `open` attribute, this approach is not recommended."

## Accessibility Claims

### ARIA Exposure

> "The `<dialog>` element is exposed by browsers in a manner similar to custom dialogs that use the ARIA [`role="dialog"`] attribute."

**Modal vs Non-Modal ARIA:**
> "`<dialog>` elements invoked by the `showModal()` method implicitly have [`aria-modal="true"`], whereas `<dialog>` elements invoked by the `show()` method or displayed using the `open` attribute or by changing the default `display` of a `<dialog>` are exposed as `[aria-modal="false"]`."

### Close Mechanism Requirement

> "Ensure a mechanism is provided to allow users to close the dialog. The most robust way to ensure that all users can close the dialog is to include an explicit button to do so, such as a confirmation, cancellation, or close button."

## CSS/Animation Claims

### Display Property Animations

> "for `<dialog>` elements to be animated the [`display`] property needs to be animatable. [Supporting browsers] animate `display` with a variation on the [discrete animation type]."

**Discrete Animation Behavior:**
> "the browser will flip between `none` and another value of `display` so that the animated content is shown for the entire animation duration."
- Entry: Flips to visible at `0%` of animation
- Exit: Flips to `none` at `100%` of animation

### Transition Requirements

Three key properties for CSS transitions:

1. **`@starting-style`** – Provides starting values for properties to transition from on every dialog open
   > "This is needed to avoid unexpected behavior. By default, CSS transitions only occur when a property changes from one value to another on a visible element; they are not triggered on elements' first style updates, or when the `display` type changes from `none` to another type."

2. **`transition-behavior: allow-discrete`** – Enables discrete transitions on `display` and `overlay`
   > "Set `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` on the `display` and `overlay` transitions (or on the [`transition`] shorthand) to enable discrete transitions on these two properties that are not by default animatable."

3. **`overlay`** Property – Ensures removal from top layer is deferred
   > "Include `overlay` in the transitions list to ensure the removal of the `<dialog>` from the top layer is deferred until the transition completes, again ensuring the transition is visible."

### Keyframe Animation Differences

> "When animating a `<dialog>` with CSS keyframe animations, there are some differences to note from transitions: You don't provide a `@starting-style`. You include the `display` value in a keyframe; this will be the `display` value for the entirety of the animation, or until another non-`none` display value is encountered."

> "You don't need to set `overlay` inside keyframes either; the `display` animation handles the animation of the `<dialog>` from shown to hidden."

### Pseudo-Classes

- **`:modal`** – Matches modal dialogs
- **`:open`** – Matches open dialogs

## Invoker Commands API

> "Modal dialogs can be declaratively opened and closed using the [Invoker Commands API] HTML attributes [`commandfor`] and [`command`], which can be set on [`<button>`] elements."

**Commands for dialogs:**
- `"show-modal"` 
- `"close"`
- `"request-close"`

Example:
```html
<button command="show-modal" commandfor="my-dialog">Open dialog</button>
<dialog id="my-dialog">
  <button commandfor="my-dialog" command="close">Close</button>
</dialog>
```

## Popover API Integration

> "Non-modal dialogs can be declaratively opened, closed, and toggled using the [Popover API] HTML attributes [`popovertarget`] and [`popovertargetaction`]."

> "The `<dialog>` must be turned into a popover by adding the `popover` attribute."

**Light Dismiss Behavior:**
> "Note that, because the dialog is a popover, it will be non-modal, so you can close it by clicking outside the dialog."

## Browser Support

**Baseline Status:**
> "This feature is well established and works across many devices and browser versions. It's been available across browsers since March 2022. \* Some parts of this feature may have varying levels of support."

---

## Key Falsifiable Claims Summary

| Claim | Falsifiability |
|-------|---|
| `showModal()` sets initial focus to first focusable element | Testable via DOM inspection |
| `showModal()` makes background inert | Testable via interaction attempts |
| Esc key closes modal with default `closedby` | Testable via keyboard event |
| Esc key does NOT close non-modal by default | Testable via keyboard event |
| `closedby="none"` blocks light dismiss | Testable via click-outside behavior |
| `form method="dialog"` closes without form submission | Testable via network monitoring |
| `display` animates with discrete type in supporting browsers | Testable via computed styles during animation |
| `@starting-style` required for transition entry | Testable by omitting and observing animation behavior |
| Modal dialog sets `aria-modal="true"` implicitly | Testable via accessibility tree inspection |
| `open` attribute creates non-modal dialog | Testable via focus trap and interaction |

claims.claim: The native <dialog> element opened with showModal() provides browser-supplied modal semantics with no JS library: the rest of the page is rendered inert, Esc dismisses it (and with stacked dialogs, Esc closes only the last-shown one), and the element is implicitly exposed as aria-modal="true" — whereas show() or the open attribute yield a non-modal dialog exposed as aria-modal="false" that does NOT dismiss on Esc by default.
claims.quote: Modal dialog boxes block interaction with other UI elements, making the rest of the page inert, while non-modal dialog boxes allow interaction with the rest of the page. ... If multiple modal dialogs are open, pressing the Esc key should close only the last shown dialog. When using `<dialog>`, this behavior is provided by the browser. ... `<dialog>` elements invoked by the `showModal()` method implicitly have `aria-modal="true"`, whereas `<dialog>` elements invoked by the `show()` method or displayed using the `open` attribute or by changing the default `display` of a `<dialog>` are exposed as `[aria-modal="false"]`. ... A non-modal dialog does not dismiss via the Esc key by default

claims.claim: Initial focus for a modal dialog defaults to the first nested focusable element; MDN prescribes using the autofocus attribute to control it explicitly, recommends the <dialog> element itself as the focus target when the best placement is unknown (e.g. dynamically rendered content), and explicitly forbids putting tabindex on the <dialog>.
claims.quote: When using [`HTMLDialogElement.showModal()`] to open a `<dialog>`, focus is set on the first nested focusable element. ... Explicitly indicating the initial focus placement by using the [`autofocus`] attribute will help ensure initial focus is set on the element deemed the best initial focus placement for any particular dialog. ... the `<dialog>` element itself may provide the best initial focus placement. ... Do not add the `tabindex` property to the `<dialog>` element as it is not interactive and does not receive focus.

claims.claim: The `closedby` attribute declaratively controls which user-initiated dismissal mechanisms a dialog accepts — "any" (light dismiss by clicking outside, plus Esc, plus developer mechanism), "closerequest" (Esc plus developer mechanism), "none" (developer mechanism only) — and when absent or invalid the dialog defaults to "closerequest" if opened with showModal() and "none" otherwise.
claims.quote: if the `<dialog>` element does not have a valid `closedby` value specified, then if it was opened using [`showModal()`], it behaves as if the value was `"closerequest"` otherwise, it behaves as if the value was `"none"`.

claims.claim: Dialog open/close motion is achievable in pure CSS with no animation runtime, but requires three specific declarations because display is a discrete-animation property: a @starting-style rule for entry values, `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` on display and overlay, and `overlay` included in the transition list so top-layer removal is deferred until the transition finishes. Keyframe animations differ: no @starting-style and no overlay are needed, and display is set inside a keyframe instead.
claims.quote: Set `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` on the `display` and `overlay` transitions (or on the [`transition`] shorthand) to enable discrete transitions on these two properties that are not by default animatable. ... Include `overlay` in the transitions list to ensure the removal of the `<dialog>` from the top layer is deferred until the transition completes, again ensuring the transition is visible. ... When animating a `<dialog>` with CSS keyframe animations, there are some differences to note from transitions: You don't provide a `@starting-style`.

claims.claim: A <form method="dialog"> (or a submit button with formmethod="dialog") closes the dialog without submitting: form control state is saved but not sent, and the dialog's returnValue is set to the activated button's value — giving a zero-JS close-and-return-a-choice pattern. The <dialog> element itself has been Baseline/available across browsers since March 2022.
claims.quote: When a `<form>` within a `<dialog>` is submitted via the `dialog` method, the dialog box closes, the states of the form controls are saved but not submitted, and the [`returnValue`] property gets set to the value of the button that was activated. ... It's been available across browsers since March 2022.
